analysis.one_liner: Caps medical malpractice awards, creates health insurance tax credits, funds electronic health records, and expands community clinics.
analysis.headline: A broad health bill from Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist and five Republican cosponsors was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill packaged several health ideas into one measure: it would cap pain-and-suffering awards in medical malpractice cases at $250,000 and tighten other lawsuit rules, while also creating a refundable, advanceable tax credit for buying private health insurance, funding a nationwide electronic health-records system, and sending grants to community health centers and children's health insurance outreach. It never got past the committee it was referred to.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured people would get a refundable tax credit paid directly to insurers to help buy coverage; children on Medicaid or SCHIP would get easier enrollment; patients in underserved areas would gain from clinic grants and a 340B drug program improvement; doctors, hospitals, and malpractice insurers would gain the most from the lawsuit caps, which limit payouts for pain and suffering and punitive damages regardless of how severe the injury.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable, advanceable tax credit for health insurance premiums, paid directly to insurance issuers so people can use it at purchase time.
Funds innovative outreach and enrollment under Medicaid and SCHIP and lets states use simplified determinations of children's financial eligibility.

Provides grants for community health centers in high-need areas, grants for integrated health care systems serving the medically underserved, improvements to the 340B drug discount program, and student-loan forbearance for volunteering at free clinics.

Establishes an Office of the National Coordinator of Health Information Technology and a public-private collaborative to build a nationwide interoperable electronic health information system, with $125 million authorized for the first year.

Keeps recovery of actual economic losses — medical bills and lost earnings — unlimited in malpractice cases while capping pain-and-suffering awards, which the bill's findings say would lower costs and improve access to care.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the insurance credits, health IT, and safety net grants. Patients injured by malpractice bear the largest direct cost: their compensation for pain, suffering, disfigurement, and loss of enjoyment of life would be capped at $250,000, awards would be reduced by any insurance benefits they receive, punitive damages would require clear-and-convincing proof of malicious or deliberate conduct, and juries would not be told the cap exists.

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages applies regardless of how many parties are liable or how catastrophic the injury, and the jury is not told about the cap; awards above it are reduced by the court.
Malpractice awards would be reduced by any collateral source benefits the claimant is entitled to, such as health or disability insurance, reducing total recovery for people who were already insured.

Punitive damages would be available only on clear and convincing evidence of malicious intent to injure or deliberate failure to avoid known injury, and could not exceed $250,000 or twice economic damages — a standard most negligence cases could never meet.
The refundable, advanceable insurance credit subsidizes purchase of private coverage without limiting premiums or guaranteeing that the credit is enough to buy meaningful coverage.

The bill creates a five-year exception to federal anti-kickback and physician self-referral laws allowing providers and hospitals to give each other health IT equipment and software, weakening those protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The coverage and safety net provisions are real but modest, and the tax credits flow through private insurers with no assurance the subsidy covers the premium. The liability provisions are the bill's center of gravity, and they transfer costs directly from malpractice insurers and providers to injured patients — capping exactly the damages (pain, suffering, lost quality of life) that fall hardest on children, the elderly, and stay-at-home parents who have little or no economic loss to claim. The package trades a known, one-sided cap on patients' recovery for speculative premium savings and uncertain coverage gains.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's Majority Leader introduced it and it went straight to the Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Frist of Tennessee, the Senate Majority Leader, introduced the bill on July 26, 2005, joined by five Republican cosponsors: Senators McConnell, Gregg, Enzi, Murkowski, and DeMint.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — was ever taken.
The bill sat in committee until the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and died without coming to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, so the status quo won. Injured patients and the plaintiffs' bar kept existing state-law remedies, while doctors, hospitals, and malpractice insurers got none of the caps they sought — and the uninsured got none of the tax credits or clinic funding either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; no one's interests moved

for.name: Sen. Bill Frist
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill, delivering introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sens. McConnell, Gregg, Enzi, Murkowski, and DeMint

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored the bill, and the Republican-run Finance Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Damage caps, punitive damage limits, and the collateral source reduction would directly shrink the payouts malpractice insurers owe, with the savings coming out of injured patients' compensation. Their gain and the public's cost are the same dollars.

industries.industry: Physicians, hospitals, and health care providers
industries.note: The liability caps would cut their malpractice exposure, and a new exception to anti-kickback and self-referral rules would let hospitals and companies donate health IT to doctors for five years. In exchange, value-based purchasing would tie a share of Medicare and Medicaid payment to measured quality, and strict expert-witness rules would make malpractice cases harder to bring.

The refundable, advanceable tax credit is paid directly to insurance issuers, routing new public subsidies through the private insurance market and locking in private insurers as the channel for federal help with coverage, without premium limits.

The bill funds a nationwide interoperable health IT infrastructure, requires federal agencies to buy only certified systems, and waives anti-kickback rules for donated systems — a large new market whose standards would also reduce medical errors for patients.

Sliding-scale caps would limit contingency fees to as little as 15 percent of large recoveries, and expert-witness and pleading restrictions would shrink the volume of health care lawsuits they can bring.

industries.industry: Community health centers and safety net clinics
industries.note: New grants for high-need community health centers and integrated care systems, 340B program improvements, and free-clinic loan forbearance would expand care for the medically underserved.
